subject: selection of parametric terms in GAM - DSM

messages.author: a428a34799cd52a2
messages.subject: selection of parametric terms in GAM - DSM
parts:
Hello everybody, 

I running a DSM to study the variables that influence the spatial distribution of territorial ungulates. My models are a mix of smooth terms and parametric (categorical) terms, for example, predation risk level (low/high).

To select smooth terms, I am using a shrinkage approach, as explained here: http://workshops.distancesampling.org/online-dsm-2020/slides/dsm3-multiple_smooths-section.pdf

My question is: what is the best way of selecting parametric terms in these DSM? Is it using p-values or maybe trying models with and without the term and assess model fit, deviance, AIC?

I apologize if this question is rather basic but I cannot find a lot of information regarding the combination of smooth and parametric terms in the literature.

Thank you very much in advance!

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] selection of parametric terms in GAM - DSM
parts:
Antonella

Fitting GAMs is not my area of expertise, so take these comments with a large pinch of salt.

Inclusion of discrete (categorical) covariates in a GAM examines whether the shape of the smooths differ among levels of the discrete covariate; in effect looking at interaction between a smooth and a discrete covariate.

Have a look at Gavin Simpson's description of a case study including both discrete covariates and smooths

https://fromthebottomoftheheap.net/2017/12/14/difference-splines-ii/

There are likely other members of the list who can offer more penetrating insights into model selection with discrete covariates.

messages.author: 350dad0a615d36db
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] selection of parametric terms in GAM - DSM
parts:
Hi Antonella, hi listfolk,

In one sense, it's fine to use p-values to do this selection.

However, if your parametric terms vary in space then you may have
problems. As illustrated in this paper,

https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~bjreich/papers/FixedEffectsYouLove.pdf

when you include a spatial random effect (e.g., a smooth of space) to
your model, you can change the effect size of parametric terms in the
model. In this case your p-values will not be "correct". This may be
especially problematic if you intend to interpret those effect sizes.
Selection via AIC or other statistics won't get around this issue. This
is somewhat of an open problem in spatial statistics, most recently
addressed in this (somewhat technical in places) paper:
https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.09420

If you don't intend to interpret the effect size (and only intend to
estimate abundance) or if your fixed effects don't vary in space then
this is less of an issue and using, say, p-values will likely be okay.

Hope this helps.

--dave
